Umbra stealth address scheme uses a dual-key system with a viewing and spending key pair for recipients.
Senders generate ephemeral keys and shared secrets to create unique stealth addresses for payments.
Umbra is deployed on Ethereum mainnet and Layer-2 networks including Polygon, Arbitrum, and Optimism.
Recipient anonymity means an adversary cannot identify the recipient better than random guessing.
Recipient unlinkability means an adversary cannot tell if two stealth payments belong to the same recipient.
The adversary model assumes full blockchain visibility but no off-chain deanonymization.
Four heuristics were identified that reduce or nullify Umbra's recipient anonymity and unlinkability.
Registrant address reuse heuristic linked 48.5% of Umbra payments on Ethereum mainnet to real recipients.
Same sender and receiver heuristic links stealth addresses used for testing or self-payments.
Collector pattern heuristic clusters stealth addresses withdrawing to the same recipient address.
Unique maxPriorityFeePerGas heuristic links withdrawals with identical unique fee settings.
On Polygon, 25.8% of Umbra payments were deanonymized using these heuristics.
On Arbitrum, 65.7% of Umbra payments were deanonymized.
On Optimism, 52.6% of Umbra payments were deanonymized.
Umbra facilitated transfers of over $155 million in crypto assets at the time of study.
Umbra requires recipients to register their public keys in a stealth key registry smart contract.
Withdrawals of ERC20 tokens from stealth addresses are done via relayers due to gas fee constraints.
The paper's code and data are open source and reproducible.
The heuristics exploit user behavior patterns rather than cryptographic weaknesses.
Umbra's stealth addresses improve privacy but practical usage patterns reduce their effectiveness.
